How Sweepstakes Casinos Work: The Dual-Currency Model Behind the Legal Fights

Published September 18, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

If you've followed this site's news coverage of state attorneys general suing sweepstakes casino operators, you've probably noticed the same phrase come up again and again: "dual-currency model." It's the mechanic these lawsuits are actually arguing about, and it's also the reason sweepstakes casinos exist at all in states where licensed, real-money online casino gambling isn't legal. Here's what the model actually is, how the math and mechanics work in practice, and why regulators increasingly see it differently than the operators do.

What a sweepstakes casino is, in plain terms

A sweepstakes casino is a website or app that offers slot-style, table-style, and sometimes live-dealer games that look and play almost identically to a real-money online casino — spinning reels, blackjack tables, roulette wheels — but is legally structured as a promotional sweepstakes rather than a gambling operation. That structure is what lets these platforms operate in states where licensed real-money online casino gambling either doesn't exist yet or is explicitly illegal, which as of 2026 is most of the country; only a handful of states have passed laws authorizing regulated real-money online casinos.

The sweepstakes framing isn't unique to gambling-style games. It's the same basic legal category as a "no purchase necessary" contest a cereal brand or fast-food chain might run, just applied to a casino-style game library instead of a single prize drawing.

The two currencies, and what each one actually does

Nearly every sweepstakes casino runs on two separate virtual currencies with different rules attached to each:

Gold Coins (the name varies by operator, but the concept is standard) have no cash value under any circumstance. They're used to play games for entertainment only, can be purchased directly for real money in packaged bundles, and can never be redeemed, cashed out, or converted back into anything of monetary worth — regardless of how much a player wins with them.

Sweeps Coins (or an equivalent second currency) are the ones that can eventually be redeemed for real cash, typically once a player accumulates enough of them and passes identity verification. Sweeps Coins are not sold directly for money — that's the legal line the whole model rests on. Instead, they're distributed as a bonus attached to a Gold Coin purchase, given out through daily login promotions, or obtainable for free through a mail-in or online request process required under sweepstakes law, often called an "alternative method of entry" or AMOE.

The core mechanic in one sentence: you can buy the currency that can't be cashed out, and you can't directly buy the currency that can — you can only receive it as a bonus, a promotion, or a free request.

The legal theory operators rely on

U.S. sweepstakes law generally permits promotions where a prize can be won without a purchase, so long as a genuinely free, reasonably accessible path to entry exists alongside any paid path. Sweepstakes casino operators argue their model satisfies this: because Sweeps Coins are never sold outright, and because a free method of obtaining them is always available (even if it's slower or less convenient than buying Gold Coins), the games qualify as a lawful sweepstakes promotion rather than a wager, even though a player can win real money.

This isn't a fringe legal theory invented recently — sweepstakes-style promotions with cash prizes have a long history in U.S. consumer marketing. What's newer is applying that framework at scale to a full casino-style game library that functions, from a player's seat, almost identically to real-money online gambling.

A worked example: one player's path through the system

Say a player buys a $20 Gold Coin package. The purchase itself is legally just buying Gold Coins for entertainment play — but as a promotional bonus tied to that purchase, the operator also credits a set number of Sweeps Coins, say 20, at no additional charge. The player can now play the same slot or table games using either currency. If they play with Gold Coins, any in-game "winnings" are just more Gold Coins, permanently unredeemable. If they play with Sweeps Coins and win, those winnings are also Sweeps Coins, and once the player's Sweeps Coin balance clears a minimum threshold and they complete identity and age verification, they can request redemption — typically arriving as a check, ACH transfer, or similar payout, often minus any required tax reporting.

A player who never wants to spend money can, in theory, request free Sweeps Coins through the operator's published AMOE process instead of buying Gold Coins, then play and redeem using only that free allotment. In practice, the free path is usually slower and yields far fewer coins per request than a paid Gold Coin package's attached bonus, which is precisely the imbalance regulators have zeroed in on.

Why regulators keep rejecting the argument

State attorneys general challenging this model generally make some version of the same core argument: that the "no purchase necessary" path is a token gesture rather than a genuinely equal alternative, and that the practical, overwhelming majority of players engage with the platform by paying for Gold Coin packages that happen to come bundled with the currency that actually matters. From that angle, regulators argue the dual-currency structure functions as a real-money wager with extra steps — you're paying for a chance at winning cash, which is the basic definition of gambling most state statutes use — dressed up in sweepstakes terminology to sidestep licensing, taxation, and consumer-protection requirements that apply to licensed real-money casinos.

That disagreement is now playing out in court and in settlement negotiations across multiple states, part of a broader wave of enforcement actions and lawsuits against sweepstakes-casino operators and their payment processors that this site's news section has tracked as it develops.

What this actually means if you're considering one

The practical risk for a player isn't just whether the model is airtight in theory — it's that the legal status of specific sweepstakes casino operators is actively being litigated state by state, and that uncertainty can affect real accounts and real balances with little warning. A platform found to be operating illegally in a given state can be ordered to stop serving residents there, and pending balances or redemption requests can be caught up in the disruption. That's a materially different risk profile than a licensed real-money online casino operating under a state gaming license, which carries direct regulatory oversight, established consumer-protection requirements, and a clear legal basis for operating in that state.

None of this means every sweepstakes casino is acting in bad faith, or that the legal question is settled in regulators' favor everywhere — it's genuinely being fought out in real time. But it's a meaningfully different category from a licensed, regulated online casino, and it's worth understanding the distinction before assuming the two work the same way. Frequently asked questions

Is it illegal to play at a sweepstakes casino?

It depends on the state and is actively being litigated. Operators argue the model is a lawful sweepstakes promotion everywhere it operates; several state attorneys general disagree and have sued specific operators, arguing the model is unlicensed gambling. There isn't a single nationwide answer as of 2026.

Can I get Sweeps Coins without ever paying anything?

Operators are generally required to offer a free method of obtaining the redeemable currency to satisfy sweepstakes law, often through a mail-in or online request process, plus periodic free bonuses like daily login credits. The free path typically delivers far fewer coins per request than a paid package's bundled bonus.

Do sweepstakes casinos report winnings for tax purposes?

Redeemed cash winnings above certain thresholds are generally subject to the same kind of tax reporting requirements as other prize or gambling winnings, and operators typically require identity verification before processing a redemption. Requirements can vary, so check the specific platform's terms and consult a tax professional for your situation.

How is this different from a social casino app that doesn't pay real money?

A pure social casino sells in-game currency for entertainment only, with no path to cash out winnings at all. A sweepstakes casino adds a second currency specifically designed to be redeemable for real money, which is the feature that puts it under gambling-law scrutiny in a way a non-redeemable social casino generally isn't.
